title: The Good, The Bad And The Ugly For Eurozone Bonds
gist: Eurozone 7-10 year government bond yields hit 3.62% on August 24, 2026 — above the 3.52% March peak reached during the Iran-war energy spike — even though crude and diesel prices remain below their March highs, which the author reads as evidence that a non-energy force (beyond inflation expectations and ECB hike pricing) is now the marginal driver of eurozone yields. Note: this record is a paywall teaser that cuts off before the author names those other forces, so the 'Good/Bad/Ugly' framing of the title is not delivered in the available text.

insights.claim: The yield on the BAML index of seven-to-10-year eurozone government bonds traced a full round trip in 2026: 2.87% on February 27, 3.52% a month later, back down to 3.19% in late June, then up to 3.62% on August 24.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: A ~75bp net rise off the February low with two violent round trips means duration in eurozone govvies has been a trading instrument, not a carry position, in 2026 — size positions for realized volatility, not for the drift.
insights.quote: the yield on the BAML index of seven-to-10-year eurozone government bonds jumped from 2.87% on February 27 to 3.52% a month later
insights.locator: So far, 2026 has been a real rollercoaster

insights.claim: The August 24, 2026 level of 3.62% on seven-to-10-year eurozone government bond yields is a new high for the year, exceeding the March peak set at the height of the energy shock.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: A break above the prior cycle high removes the technical argument that March marked the yield ceiling; treat 3.52% as support-turned-resistance rather than a cap.
insights.locator: Since then, yields have climbed again

themes.theme: Iran war as the energy-to-yields transmission channel

insights.claim: The start of the Iran war pushed energy prices higher and was the proximate cause of the roughly 65bp jump in seven-to-10-year eurozone government bond yields between late February and late March 2026.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Establishes a quantified geopolitical-risk transmission chain (Middle East conflict to European energy to European duration) that can be used to size hedges against future escalation headlines.
insights.locator: As the start of the Iran war pushed energy prices higher

insights.claim: The subsequent retreat in energy prices was followed by eurozone seven-to-10-year yields falling roughly 33bp over three months to 3.19% in late June, confirming the energy-price channel worked symmetrically on the way down.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: The clean two-way linkage through mid-2026 is what makes the post-June breakdown in that relationship diagnostically meaningful rather than noise.

themes.theme: Energy no longer explains the yield move

insights.claim: Crude oil and diesel prices are both below their March 2026 peaks even as eurozone sovereign yields trade well above their March high, breaking the energy-price-to-yield relationship that held earlier in the year.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: The core actionable observation: investors modelling eurozone duration off an oil-price input are now using a broken model and will misprice the next leg.
insights.quote: In contrast, eurozone sovereign bond yields are now well above their March high. This suggests that there are other forces beyond energy prices driving up eurozone yields.
insights.locator: But broadly, energy prices remain below their March highs

insights.claim: Wholesale natural gas prices are the one energy component above their March 2026 peak, making European gas — not oil or diesel — the only remaining energy-side justification for the yield move.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: European gas is the specific energy series to watch for a residual inflation-expectations impulse into Bund and OAT yields; oil is now a red herring for this trade.
insights.quote: although wholesale prices for natural gas are up
insights.locator: crude oil and diesel, for example, are down

insights.claim: An unidentified non-energy force has become the marginal driver of eurozone government bond yields since late June 2026, implying the yield rise is no longer purely an inflation-expectations story.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: If the driver is term premium, fiscal supply or credit risk rather than inflation, then a fall in energy prices will not rescue long eurozone duration — and the usual disinflation trade will fail.
insights.locator: This suggests that there are other forces

insights.claim: The pickup in energy prices since late June 2026 has pushed inflation expectations higher and led markets to price in additional European Central Bank rate hikes.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: The ECB is being priced for further tightening, not cuts — a hawkish front-end setup that argues against receiving European rates on a disinflation view alone.
insights.locator: Yes, energy prices have also picked up since late June
